items.title: Protecting birds in protected areas: a multi-scale analysis of forest structure and species occurrence
items.abstract: Context Protected areas are cornerstones of avian conservation, yet forest-associated bird communities continue to decline even within protected lands. The capacity of a protected area to sustain bird populations depends on both internal habitat quality and the surrounding landscape context, yet the relative importance of these scales remains poorly understood. Objectives We evaluate how forest structure at three nested spatial scales (local, park, and county) influences the occurrence of forest-associated birds within protected areas. Methods We analyzed 17 years (2006–2023) of point count data for 16 forest-bird species across eight National Parks in the Northeastern United States to determine the relationships between species occurrences and five forest-structure variables, including the dominant spatial scale for each. Forest-structure variables were derived at local, park, and county spatial scales using long-term park monitoring and national forest inventory data. Results County-scale forest variables were selected most frequently as the dominant scale of effect on bird occurrence probabilities (19 species-covariate combinations), followed by local (16) and park (5) scales, with at least one county-scale forest variable influencing 75% of species. All but two species showed significant associations with forest structure variables. Park size had weak and inconsistent effects on occurrence, likely because the parks included in our study are all small. While these parks contain quality avian habitat, county-scale forest availability and connectivity may constrain which species persist within them. Conclusions Protected areas cannot conserve forest-associated birds in isolation; regional landscape context at the county-scale is an equally important determinant of species occurrences, especially for small, protected areas. Management of the matrix habitat surrounding protected areas, such as restoring forest availability and improving connectivity, may yield greater conservation returns than management of protected areas in isolation. This can be a tractable strategy for practitioners in regions where expanding formal protection is constrained by competing land uses.

items.title: How do we know when invasive species control strategies work?
items.abstract: Controlling invasive species is costly and difficult but can have major ecological, economic, and health benefits. Researchers commonly compare the efficacy of specific control methods. However, invasive species control programs vary greatly in overarching goals and often occur over large areas, long timeframes, and varied environmental and social contexts. The success of these programs likely hinges on factors including organizational structures, concurrent restoration activities, geographic and temporal scope of control, and the invasive species’ biology. To enable assessment of the relative influence of these common features, we propose clearer definitions of success in invasive species control and explicit comparisons among control programs. Post hoc assessment of existing programs’ success will complement system-specific studies to guide strategies that work in real-world situations.

items.title: Global Patterns in the Nutrient Composition Delivered by Seabirds to Coastal and Island Ecosystems
items.abstract: Aim Consumer‐mediated nutrient dynamics are crucial for sustaining ecosystems. While most research has focused on the magnitude of seabird‐derived nutrient fluxes, the role of species and diet composition in shaping nutrient quality remains largely unexplored. We aim to test whether the stoichiometric composition of seabird‐derived nutrient subsidies is spatially structured. Location Global. Time Period 1950–2025. Major Taxa Studied Seabirds: Charadriiformes, Pelecaniformes, Phaethontiformes, Procellariiformes, Sphenisciformes and Suliformes. Methods Using dietary data and prey nutrient stoichiometry, we quantified nitrogen and phosphorus excretion for 166 seabird species and analysed variation in excreta nitrogen:phosphorus (N:P) ratios across geographic gradients. Spatial patterns were assessed at three scales: (i) species centroid distributions; (ii) global patterns weighted by breeding abundance at the grid‐cell level (141 species); and (iii) continental patterns weighted by breeding abundance at the colony level (79 species). Results Excreta N:P ratios showed a strong latitudinal gradient, declining from southern high latitudes towards the tropics. Abundance‐weighted analyses confirmed this pattern at both global and continental scales, with increased nitrogen enrichment in Arctic regions, although less pronounced than in the Southern Ocean. Stoichiometry varied strongly across climate zones, with greater stoichiometric variability in polar and subpolar regions than in the tropics. Taxonomic identity and diet composition were the strongest predictors of excretion stoichiometry, but geographical patterns contributed substantially. Main Conclusions Consistent with ecological stoichiometry, species identity and diet are primary drivers of seabird nutrient composition. Spatial patterns identify regions of high stoichiometric variability that are likely sensitive to shifts in prey availability and species redistribution under climate change. N:P ratios of deposited excreta broadly align with marine nutrient limitation patterns but contrast terrestrial plant limitation, delivering relatively P‐rich subsidies in tropical regions and N‐rich inputs at high latitudes. These results demonstrate that seabirds impose a spatial structure on cross‐ecosystem nutrient subsidies, linking marine and terrestrial nutrient regimes. Changes in seabird distributions and abundance are therefore likely to alter both the magnitude and composition of nutrient inputs, with consequences for island ecosystem functioning.

items.title: Primary and secondary invasion pathways: why the distinction matters
items.abstract: The pathways by which non-native species are introduced and spread shape the rate and geographic patterns of biological invasions. They can be classified as primary, where species cross jurisdictional or biogeographic boundaries, or secondary, where they move within those boundaries after introduction. Despite economic, political, social, and ecological differences between these pathway types, most classification schemes and regulatory frameworks do not explicitly distinguish between them. Primary pathways are relatively well-defined and subject to biosecurity regulation, while secondary pathways remain poorly characterized and largely overlooked in policy and practice. Secondary pathways create multiple nodes from which species spread, complicating containment. Here we refine the distinction between primary and secondary pathways and explore how failing to recognize this distinction can limit the effectiveness of biosecurity systems, particularly by leaving secondary pathways inadequately addressed. Distinguishing between primary and secondary pathways can improve control responses, strengthen cross-scale coordination, reduce economic damage, and support global biodiversity targets.

items.title: No biotic homogenization in the understory of Cupressus sempervirens long-established plantations
items.abstract: Non-native species spreading naturally are associated with losses of native diversity and biotic homogenization. Conversely, the effect of non-native tree species used in plantations may vary, particularly according to their biogeographical origin. We investigated whether the canopy cover of Cupressus sempervirens long-established plantations affects alpha and beta taxonomic diversity of understory plant communities, alters their functional composition, or promotes disturbance-related species. We surveyed 74 plots in cypress plantations along a latitudinal gradient in Italy. We used beta-dispersion analysis and regression models to test the effect of cypress cover and environmental conditions on understory vegetation. We found no influence of cypress cover on soil conditions and no evidence of cypress-driven taxonomic homogenization. Understory diversity and composition were unrelated to cypress cover but formed three site-specific groups reflecting local environmental conditions. Likewise, cypress cover did not affect understory functional composition, although it varied across sites. Disturbance indicator values showed no significant variation along cypress cover or among sites, indicating no ruderalization. Long-established non-native plantations of C. sempervirens function as unmanaged, naturalized forests in which cypress exerts little to no influence on understory plant diversity and composition, even at high cover. This could be attributed to the vertical crown structure of C. sempervirens that allows light to reach the forest floor, to the biogeographic origin of Mediterranean cypress, and to the presence of native tree species in the canopy. Our results indicate that long-established C. sempervirens plantations can retain ecological value. However, this should not be taken as a justification for the indiscriminate establishment of new plantations, as their ecological effects may vary depending on ecosystem complexity.

items.title: Fifteen years of change in biodiversity conservation across Latin America and the Caribbean
items.abstract: Latin America and the Caribbean (LACA) is one of the most biodiverse regions globally, yet it continues to experience accelerated biodiversity loss driven by persistent and emerging anthropogenic pressures. In 2009, the Society for Conservation Biology conducted a regional assessment of conservation challenges; however, the evolution of these dynamics over the following 15 years had not been systematically reassessed. We conducted an updated regional synthesis of biodiversity conservation priorities, perceived threats, and implementation barriers across 25 countries, based on a 2024 survey of conservation professionals (n = 244). Respondents were predominantly experienced practitioners affiliated with academic institutions, nongovernmental organizations, and government agencies. Our findings were consistent with the patterns reported in 2009, with deforestation, habitat fragmentation, industrial agriculture, climate change, and pollution persisting as the most severe threats. However, these traditional drivers are now compounded by the intensification of landscape-scale pressures and a marked shift toward the security-conservation nexus. Respondents explicitly identified organized crime and drug trafficking as primary constraints that compromise both ecosystem integrity and the safety of practitioners. Although conservation tools, such as protected areas and environmental policies, have diversified and improved in many ways, their effectiveness remains limited by a diversification without consolidation trend, characterized by chronic underfunding, corruption, and weak intersectoral coordination. Furthermore, engagement with local communities and citizen science remains predominantly low to moderate, highlighting an enduring gap between policy design and on-the-ground implementation. This study underscores that addressing biodiversity loss in LACA has moved beyond the need for technical solutions; it now requires a fundamental transformation in governance quality, institutional integrity, and state capacity to protect the region's natural heritage and the communities that depend on it.

items.title: Global drivers of invasive and native plant niche breadth within plant-floral visitor interaction networks
items.abstract: Plant invasions are of major ecological concern due to their negative effects on local communities, posing a threat to native plant diversity through competition for resources. Particularly, invasive species’ impacts on plant-pollinator interactions can have important consequences for native plant fitness, as well as exert neutral or facilitative effects on these mutualistic interactions. The niche breadth, understood as the variety of resources used by a species, can be related in this case to the magnitude and direction of invaders’ impacts on recipient plant communities. However, a comprehensive understanding of which factors shape the invasive plants’ niche breadth globally remains limited. To address this gap, we investigated the global drivers of invasive and native plants’ niche breadth based on two complementary metrics. To do that, we compiled a global dataset of weighted plant-floral visitor interaction networks that included invasive plants and estimated species specialization ( d’ ) and normalized degree for invasive and native plants. Moreover, we assessed the influence of climate and geographical factors on both metrics using LMM models. Our results revealed that temperature, precipitation, insularity, and latitude emerged as key predictors of specialization, and that temperature, latitude, and web intensity shaped the normalized degree for both plant groups. However, invasive status did not have a significant effect on either niche-breadth metric, and no interaction with the other drivers turned out to be significant. Our findings highlight the strong influence of environmental and geographical factors on plants’ niche breadth; this is especially relevant considering the current climate change context.

items.title: The interplay of landscape connectivity, composition and configuration in alien plant invasions across an ecological network
items.abstract: Context Biological invasions are deemed to be the second most important global driver of biodiversity loss showing strong interactions with the aftermaths of land use change and landscape fragmentation. The role of landscape composition and configuration in biological invasions is widely considered while its interplay with landscape connectivity is less understood. However, ecological connectivity can be equally crucial for both native and alien species, constituting the backbone of ecological network initiatives. Objectives We aim to assess how landscape composition, configuration and connectivity (in the ecological network) influence α- and β-diversity (floristic uniqueness) of both alien and native plant species, and to determine whether these effects differ according to habitat type. Methods The study was conducted in a 298 km 2 ecological network in the lowlands of Friuli Venezia Giulia, northeastern Italy, encompassing a mosaic of agricultural, natural, and semi-natural habitats. A hierarchical sampling design was applied to 87 terrestrial habitat nodes, where plant species composition and abundance were recorded in 219 plots. Landscape composition, configuration and connectivity were quantified to examine their influence on native and alien plant α- and β-diversity across different habitat types. Results We found contrasting effects of landscape connectivity, composition and configuration for native and alien species. Peripheral, less connected sites favored native species richness (α-diversity) and contributed to maintaining native floristic uniqueness (high β-diversity). In contrast, alien species richness was mainly associated with landscape composition and configuration, particularly the proportion of natural land use and edge-related effects in wooded habitats, while plots with higher alien richness showed lower compositional uniqueness within the alien species pool. Landscape composition and configuration also influenced invasion dynamics, as nodes surrounded by a high proportion of natural land uses with simple shapes helped contain plant invasions while preserving native richness and uniqueness. These patterns were often habitat-dependent, with stronger effects observed in wooded areas, where alien α-diversity increased with fragmentation, whereas native species richness declined. Conclusions Our findings suggest that managing landscape connectivity and reducing fragmentation can enhance resistance to invasions and support native species richness. Peripheral nodes may act as native refugia, supporting high native richness and floristic uniqueness, while more accessible central nodes may function as alien hubs associated with greater alien compositional uniqueness and potential propagule exchange. Shifting from intensive to extensive land uses through green infrastructures provides a win–win strategy, promoting native species and limit alien establishment.

items.title: A multi-scale approach for understanding factors limiting invasive carp distribution in the Ohio River Basin
items.abstract: The spread of aquatic invasive species (AIS) poses a major threat to freshwater biodiversity. Understanding the mechanisms regulating occurrence of invasive species in invaded systems requires a multi-scale approach, as regional dispersal can facilitate arrival while local processes ultimately determine their persistence across a landscape. We used a dynamic multi-scale occupancy model to test hypothesized factors limiting the occurrence of invasive bigheaded carps (bighead carp Hypophthalmichthys nobilis and silver carp H. molitrix ) in the Ohio River, USA. Across the basin, invasion has slowed, with limited evidence of upstream advancement of their invaded range in this system. However, once present, silver carp and bighead carp populations tended to persist even in apparently low numbers. Bighead carp occurrence was not correlated with any environmental variables. On the local scale, silver carp exhibit clear habitat and flow preferences, where populations persisted in low velocity off-channel locations especially when flows are too high in the main channel. We found evidence for decreasing detection of both species in mid-reach and upstream pools, potentially because of lower abundance in these reaches. Our results indicated that while silver carp occurred throughout a large range of the Ohio River, fewer sites were occupied in upstream reaches. However, there was indirect evidence that site-level occurrence was increasing in the invasion front. Understanding these multi-scale dynamics can be helpful for developing effective strategies to contain invasive silver carp and bighead carp in the Ohio River and other systems.

items.title: Mapping and conservation analysis of upper montane evergreen broad‐leaved forest using machine learning and geodata
items.abstract: The upper montane evergreen broad‐leaved forest (UMEBLF) provides unique ecological functions but exhibits a highly fragmented spatial distribution. Mapping the suitable habitat of UMEBLF and assessing its conservation status are therefore crucial for regional protection and management of this vegetation. In this study, Yunnan Province, China, was used as a case study and employed 11 topographic and climatic variables, including mountain relative height, to identify an optimal Random Forest model for simulating and mapping the suitable distribution of UMEBLF under current and future climate scenarios. In addition, the montane cloud–fog belt within the monsoon core region was incorporated to evaluate the reliability of the mapping results under current climatic conditions. By comparing the spatial distribution of nature reserves across the province, the current protection status of UMEBLF and its potential future changes were clarified. Results indicate that under current climatic conditions, areas with high habitat suitability for UMEBLF cover approximately 4.2 × 10 4 km 2 , primarily distributed across the mid‐montane zones of western and central Yunnan. The lower boundary of suitable habitat closely coincides with the elevation of the cloud–fog belt and is primarily located on middle to upper slopes, at approximately two‐thirds of the mountain's relative height above the base surface. Under future warming scenarios, the spatial pattern of suitable habitat exhibits relatively stable core areas and highly dynamic marginal zones. Under the SSP5‐8.5 scenario, the area of highly suitable habitat is projected to decline to approximately 3.0 × 10 4 km 2 by the 2090s. Currently, 32 nature reserves contain areas with high habitat suitability, with 75% concentrated on the southwestern side of the Cangshan–Ailao Mountain region. In the future, the proportion of highly suitable habitat areas within protected zones is expected to decrease by 15.9%–18.7%, with reductions occurring mainly within experimental zones of nature reserves. This study demonstrates an integrated framework combining geospatial big data and machine learning to map and analyze UMEBLF distribution, providing a scientific basis for mountain forest conservation and management under climate change.

items.title: Disentangling the interactive effects of anthropogenic disturbances on biodiversity
items.abstract: Anthropogenic activity threatens biodiversity through climate change, habitat fragmentation, and increasing frequency and scale of disturbance. Various theoretical studies have sought to shed light on how these factors could promote or hinder the coexistence of species. However, our understanding of the relative importance of, and interactions between, these factors remains limited. In this study, we employ a theoretical approach integrating three commonly cited coexistence mechanisms – the competition–colonisation trade‐off, the intermediate disturbance hypothesis, and habitat fragmentation – into a unified model. We implement a novel method to integrate habitat structure into a system of differential equations, to create a simple and flexible model that can be used to investigate coexistence of multiple species arranged in a competitive hierarchy under different disturbance and habitat structure scenarios. Using this model, we find that considering interactions between different mechanisms is crucial for explaining the coexistence of species. Biodiversity patterns alternative to the uni‐peak curve predicted by the intermediate disturbance hypothesis (e.g. bimodal) emerge along disturbance gradients as habitat fragmentation increases. Furthermore, habitat loss outweighs spatial isolation effects in highly disturbed scenarios, yet isolation can shape species coexistence under low disturbance. These findings underscore the need to integrate spatial and temporal mechanisms in biodiversity management.

items.title: The science-policy gap on invasive species management: a review of research capacity, regulations, and data availability for an intergovernmental framework in the gulf cooperation council
items.abstract: Invasive alien species (IAS) pose major threats to biodiversity, ecosystem function, and agriculture, undermining progress on the Sustainable Development Goals. The Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC), with its arid climate, rapid urbanisation, dependence on imports, and ecologically fragile, endemic-rich habitats, is especially vulnerable. This paper constructs bridges over the science–policy gap in invasive species management through a systematic review of national and regional regulatory frameworks, global invasion ecology publications, and 3.9 million biodiversity records. GCC institutions contribute only 0.6% of global invasion-ecology publications and, when normalised by GDP, produce invasion science at less than one-third of the global rate. Across the GCC, only 84 of 707 GRIIS-listed IAS (11.9%) are regulated, despite significant economic impacts. Critical deficiencies include species-specific laws, pathway controls, enforcement, and cross-border coordination, as most nations address invasive species only within broader biodiversity strategies. To remedy this, we propose an Inter-Governmental Invasive Species Science-Policy Platform (IISSPP), modelled on the Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services (IPBES), a lean intergovernmental science–policy platform built around regular assessments, early warning and knowledge generation, policy support, and capacity building. IISSPP would harmonise regulations, standardise risk assessments, unify watch lists, and promote open data sharing. The IISSPP model is replicable in other rapidly developing regions and supports global biodiversity targets under the Kunming–Montreal Framework while advancing regional sustainable development and climate resilience.

items.title: “Alligator weed” on the radar: where are we now and where should we go?
items.abstract: Alternanthera philoxeroides (APs), a globally invasive perennial weed, threatens agriculture and ecosystems owing to its rapid clonal spread and strong adaptability. Despite extensive research on APs biology and management, a bibliometric synthesis that systematically maps the intellectual structure and evolving research fronts of this field has not yet been conducted. To address this gap, a bibliometric analysis was performed on 833 APs-related publications from 1943 to 2025 using VOSviewer and CiteSpace. Results show that APs research has gained increasing attention, with China as the most productive country, the Chinese Academy of Sciences as the most productive institution, and Feihai Yu as the most prolific author. “Plant Sciences” was the most represented category, with Frontiers in Plant Science and Journal of Aquatic Plant Management as the most productive journals. Four research hotspots were identified: (1) invasive biological traits (clonal integration and epigenetic plasticity); (2) control strategies (biological and chemical); (3) tolerance mechanisms and remediation applications under heavy metal and salt stress; and (4) invasion dynamics under climate change. Three emerging frontiers were identified as model-based distribution forecasting to inform biological control decisions, disturbance-defense feedback mechanisms, and resource utilization for agricultural quality enhancement and environmental benefits. Future research should address synergistic effects of multiple stressors (e.g., elevated CO₂, UV-B, and microplastics) and integrate remote sensing, geographic information systems (GIS), and Global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSS) with biomolecular tools to support adaptive management frameworks.

items.title: Integrating land-use and climate connectivity to link protected areas at the country level
items.abstract: Context Ecological corridors that are high in biodiversity potential and stable under climate change are central to long-term conservation planning. Yet spatial prioritization frameworks rarely integrate land-use resistance and climate stability into a unified approach, limiting their operational value for landscape management and policy. Objectives We aimed to develop an ecological connectivity framework that jointly incorporates land-use resistance and climate stability to map linkages among protected areas, and to quantify and communicate methodological uncertainty arising from key parameterization choices. Methods We applied the framework to Portugal's terrestrial protected-area network. Using a full factorial design, we varied land-use resistance, climate resistance, and dispersal capacity across multiple weightings to generate optimized linkage solutions. Selection-frequency maps derived from these solutions fed a second optimization round, producing an ensemble connectivity solution and buffered corridors. Results Individual solutions covered 0.74% of Portugal's unprotected land; the ensemble covered 0.07%, rising to 2.3% after a 1 km buffer. Dispersal capacity parameterization introduced greater uncertainty in connectivity outcomes than land-use or climate resistance scores, suggesting it deserves particular attention in future studies. Protected areas in the Central–North region emerged as the most critical network hubs, with the highest centrality under both resistance gradients. The ensemble highlighted areas of high concordance across parameterizations, improving the robustness of spatial priorities. Conclusions Integrating land-use and climate resistance identifies corridors that are both functional and climate-resilient. Explicitly mapping uncertainty and producing ensemble-prioritized linkages improves the reliability of spatial recommendations, offering planners a practical tool for embedding connectivity targets into conservation and land management decisions.

items.title: A standardized workflow for compiling and harmonizing first records of non-native species
items.abstract: NeoBiota 110: 1-20 DOI: 10.3897/neobiota.110.198728 Authors: Tanara Renard Truong, Franz Essl, Hanno Seebens Abstract: Biological invasions are a major driver of biodiversity loss, and tracking non-native species introductions is essential for biodiversity monitoring and policy assessment. First records, defined as the earliest documented evidence of a species occurring in the wild outside its native range, provide a standardized metric to quantify introduction dynamics across regions and taxonomic groups. However, compiling and harmonizing such records from diverse sources remain challenging due to non-standardized terminology and heterogeneous reporting standards. Here, we describe a reproducible workflow for standardizing first records of non-native species from diverse sources. The workflow is implemented in R and is designed to ensure consistency in taxonomy, harmonize geographic locations, convert heterogeneous temporal expressions into four-digit years using explicit transformation rules, and standardize terms following Darwin Core terminology. A key innovation of the workflow is the assignment of a confidence level to each standardized first record, reflecting the uncertainty of the original temporal information. The workflow is open-source, modular, and customizable, allowing users to apply it to their own data or modify standardization rules. It is applied to produce v4.0 of the FirstRecords dataset, which contains nearly 100,000 first records of more than 30,000 taxa and is structured into linked tables covering actual records, taxonomy, locations, and data sources. This represents a 17.8% increase in the amount of available first records compared to the previous version, of which approximately 8% is due to the refinement of the workflow. By providing a transparent and automated approach to data harmonization, this workflow facilitates large-scale analyses of invasion patterns and indicator development, while maintaining data integrity. items.title: Spatial and historical effects shape a wide‐scale rice field ostracod metacommunity pervaded by invasive species
items.abstract: Metacommunity structure is shaped by a complex interplay of environmental conditions, spatial factors, and historical contingencies. To determine the processes that govern community assembly and biodiversity patterns, it is necessary to know the relative importance of these elements. In this study, we examine the ostracod metacommunity of rice fields across the Iberian Peninsula, aiming to assess the influence of spatial constraints, historical contingency (as derived from taphocoenoses remains), and environmental variables on the present metacommunity (biocoenoses) structure. We hypothesized that while all three components would affect the metacommunity, spatial effects would be particularly relevant due to the large geographical scope and associated dispersal limitations. Our results indicate that space was the most relevant factor in structuring the metacommunity, operating at broad and fine scales. Historical contingency also contributed substantially, as indicated by the high concordance between taphocoenoses and biocoenoses, suggesting that past community composition influences present assemblages, possibly through colonization advantages associated with egg banks. Although the pure environmental fraction was comparatively weak and nonsignificant, likely due to the low environmental variability of these homogeneous and artificially controlled aquatic habitats, the substantial shared environmental-spatial fraction could indicate that environmental conditions covaried with broad-scale spatial structure among regions. A notable number of invasive ostracods were identified, suggesting ongoing, albeit infrequent, colonization processes, probably facilitated by waterbirds, land ploughing, movement of agricultural machinery, and farmer activities, which support the establishment of invasive species within each community egg bank. These findings indicate that biodiversity management in seasonal agricultural landscapes, such as rice fields, should extend beyond local environmental conditions, taking into account regional connectivity, the persistence of egg-bank legacies, and human-mediated dispersal pathways that may facilitate the establishment of non-native species.

items.title: Modelling habitat suitability for multiple priority weed species to predict invasion hotspots for strategic management in complex landscapes
items.abstract: Established weeds require ongoing, costly management to reduce harm to agricultural and environmental values. Heterogeneous landscapes that encompass substantial variation in land use, vegetation and topographic conditions are often under threat from multiple long-established weeds, whose simultaneous management presents strategic and tactical challenges. Systematic monitoring of weed populations provides more detailed insights into invasion threats than the more readily available presence-only data. We leveraged six years of weed density monitoring and high-resolution environmental data to model habitat suitability for four high-priority weeds across the Australian Capital Territory. We developed habitat suitability maps for African lovegrass, Chilean needlegrass, serrated tussock grass and St John’s wort. Maps were then standardised and combined to derive potential multi-species invasion hotspots and explore patterns of secondary invasion threat. While some species shared environmental predictors such as elevation, each responded to distinct combinations and interactions among environmental predictors. Overall, we found approximately 71% of the study area was suitable for multiple weeds to exceed low densities, but only 11% was sufficiently suitable for two or more species to reach high densities. In those invasion hotspots, habitat suitability was often highest for St John’s wort, and where suitability was highest for either of the other three weeds, St John’s wort typically posed the second highest invasion threat. These findings could improve management efficiency by focussing integrated control of multiple co-occurring species in a small number of priority invasion hotspots. Our study demonstrates how spatially explicit models and analyses based on systematically collected weed density data can inform a multi-species, landscape-scale approach to weed management.

items.title: Resource subsidies mediated by non-native species: a review
items.abstract: NeoBiota 109: 315-343 DOI: 10.3897/neobiota.109.193175 Authors: Letícia Alves, Janeide Padilha, Phillip J. Haubrock, Amanda Subalusky, Ronaldo Sousa Abstract: Non-native species are recognized as one of the major drivers of biodiversity change globally, with profound impacts on ecosystem functions and services. Despite the high number of studies on non-native species published, mainly in the last two decades, an often-overlooked aspect is their role as mediators of resource subsidies (the cross-boundary movement of energy, nutrients, or materials). This topic may have theoretical and empirical implications because non-native species may play a major role in ecosystem connectivity by transporting—or interrupting the transport of—energy and organic matter. Therefore, the main aims of this review were to (1) assess temporal trends, geographic distribution, and methodological approaches in research on resource subsidies mediated by non-native species; (2) synthesize how non-native species alter the magnitude, direction, and dynamics of resource subsidies across ecosystems and their implications for ecosystem functioning; and (3) identify key gaps in current knowledge and define future research priorities. The review retrieved 143 publications, resulting in 212 case studies, that collectively show that non-native species can both reduce and increase resource flows across ecosystem boundaries, with implications for ecosystem dynamics and connectivity. Although terrestrial and freshwater connectivity accounted for the majority of published case studies (56%), many ecosystem linkages remain underexplored. A significant geographic bias was found, with Africa being severely understudied (2.8% of all publications), followed by Asia (7.7% of all publications). Taxonomic representation was also skewed, with the majority of studies focusing on non-native plants (28.8% of case studies), non-native fish (25.5% of case studies), and mammals (21.7% of case studies), whereas fungi (0.9%) and bacteria (2.4%) were largely neglected despite their fundamental roles in decomposition processes. Key priorities for advancing this field include long-term monitoring, the application of emerging molecular and analytical tools (e.g., telemetry, eDNA, metabarcoding, and isotopic tracers), and the integration of artificial intelligence to synthesize large datasets. The findings provide the first synthesis of resource subsidies mediated by non-native species. This information is crucial for biodiversity conservation and the effective management of ecosystems and their connectivity. HTML XML PDF

items.title: Effects of climate change on marine biodiversity on the western Atlantic coast
items.abstract: The current climate crisis, driven by greenhouse gas emissions, threatens global biodiversity, including that in marine ecosystems. However, projections for the western Atlantic Ocean that jointly quantify species richness and endemism while accounting for spatially biased and incomplete occurrence data remain limited. We addressed this gap across the western Atlantic from 57°S to 40°N, within 1500 km of the coast and on the continental shelf in waters shallower than 150 m. Using broad taxonomic coverage across vertebrates, invertebrates, and algae, we modeled biodiversity metrics directly as species richness and the corrected weighted endemism index (WEIc), applied uniform sampling from sampling effort (USSE) to minimize the effects of spatially biased and incomplete occurrence records on predictions, and tested multiple algorithms to project these metrics under Shared Socioeconomic Pathway (SSP) scenarios SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5 for 2050 and 2100. The results indicated a significant reduction in species richness and endemism, with up to 69% of the study area projected to experience a reduction of more than 5% in species richness under the high-emissions scenarios. The most affected areas included the coast of Florida, the Gulf of Mexico, the Caribbean, the northern region of South America, and southern Brazil. The decrease in endemism was equally concerning, with significant reductions predicted in areas of high diversity, threatening species adapted to specific ecological niches and increasing the risk of local extinctions. Vertebrates and invertebrates showed the greatest reductions in richness in the Gulf of Mexico, the Caribbean, northeastern Brazil, and northern Argentina. For algae, the most significant decreases were predicted for Florida and southern Brazil. This loss of biodiversity could compromise the resilience of marine ecosystems and the availability of fishery resources, highlighting the urgent need for coordinated global actions.

items.title: Ecosystem service gradients at protected area borders reveal multiple patterns and prevalent management conflicts
items.abstract: Protected areas cannot halt biodiversity loss in isolation; integrating them with surrounding human-dominated landscapes is critical. However, this integration is challenged by substantial landscape heterogeneity at protected area borders, making it difficult to determine cross-border changes in ecosystem service provision. To address this knowledge gap, we developed a novel framework for characterizing these dynamics by analyzing ecosystem service gradients along protected area borders. For 16 protected areas in the French Alps, we used a mix of established biophysical models and novel connectivity-based models for mobile species to assess 12 ecosystem services. These services were aggregated into three stakeholder-driven domains reflecting rural, cultural, and urban management priorities. Automated polynomial regression analysis classified borders into five gradient types. The most common types were decreasing gradients, representing a decline in ecosystem services outside the protected area, and increasing gradients with the opposite pattern. Our analysis revealed that these patterns are driven by specific landscape configurations and uncovered frequent trade-offs between the three management priorities; for example, landscapes supporting rural priorities often degrade cultural and urban ones. We also identified key opportunities for synergies by identifying areas where ecosystem services for all three priority domains increased simultaneously outside the protected area. This spatially explicit typology provides a powerful diagnostic tool for designing targeted interventions, such as prioritizing habitat restoration where ecosystem services decline or managing agricultural landscapes to mitigate conflicts across management priorities, supporting a more effective integration of protected areas into the wider landscape.

items.title: Optimizing ecological security patterns in western Jilin, China: comparative ecological source identification and explainable machine-learning resistance modeling
items.abstract: Context Agricultural expansion and landscape fragmentation are altering ecological connectivity in agro-pastoral transition zones. Ecological security patterns can support landscape conservation and restoration, but their reliability is constrained by uncertainty in ecological source identification and resistance surface construction. Objectives This study identified suitable methods for constructing ecological security patterns in ecologically fragile agricultural landscapes. We compared three ecological source identification approaches and five machine learning models for resistance surface construction, and assessed their implications for ecological network optimization in western Jilin, China. Methods We assessed five ecosystem services and compared ordered weighted averaging, morphological spatial pattern analysis, and ecosystem service significance assessment for ecological source identification. We compared five machine learning models to construct the ecological resistance surface. Based on the selected sources and resistance surface, we used minimum cumulative resistance and circuit theory to identify corridors, pinch points, and barriers. Results Ecosystem services showed spatial heterogeneity, with most services decreasing from east to west. Scenario 4 of ordered weighted averaging (OWA4) achieved the highest conservation efficiency for biodiversity, Ramsar wetlands, and nature reserves, whereas morphological spatial pattern analysis (MSPA) provided the greatest coverage of these elements. Given its higher conservation efficiency and more balanced representation of multiple ecosystem services, OWA4 was selected for subsequent connectivity planning. RF and XGBoost showed the strongest overall performance; RF achieved the higher AUC, whereas XGBoost provided a more balanced representation of resistance factors. Both were retained for resistance surface construction. The final ecological security pattern included 23 ecological sources covering 3719.62 km 2 , 30 corridors, 243 pinch points, and 31 barrier areas. Urban areas, croplands, roads, and saline-alkali lands were major constraints on ecological flows. Conclusions Integrating comparative source identification, machine learning-based resistance modeling, and circuit theory reduced uncertainty in ecological security pattern construction. The resulting “two corridors, two belts, and three zones” framework can guide wetland restoration, corridor protection, and landscape planning in agricultural-wetland landscapes.

items.title: Regional tree migration outpaces local migration due to fragmentation and life history traits
items.abstract: Context Predictions of tree species range shifts have emphasized regional migration rates, while how local migration drives regional migration remains poorly understood. Landscape fragmentation is a major source of migration lag, but its interactions with species life history traits remain understudied. Objectives We aimed to clarify mechanisms underlying differences between local and regional migration rates, quantify how fragmentation and life history traits jointly shape migration, and assess temporal variation in these effects. Methods We quantified local and regional migration rates of temperate tree species with contrasting life history traits across fragmented landscapes. LANDIS PRO incorporated key demographic processes, including seed dispersal, colonization, establishment, growth, and mortality. We assessed direct and interactive effects of fragmentation over short (0–30 years), medium (30–65 years), and long (65–100 years) timescales. Results Regional migration was nearly five times faster than local migration, and increasing fragmentation reduced regional migration and increased migration lags. Fragmentation more strongly constrained regional migration, whereas, among the six focal species, life history traits such as maturity age and seed production showed stronger associations with local migration. Direct effects dominated in the short term, but interactive effects became increasingly important over time, consistent with accumulating demographic delays in fragmented landscapes. Conclusions Our results show that patch dynamics help explain why regional migration outpaces local migration, but reliance on regional leading-edge migration rates alone could overestimate assisted-migration distances. Comparisons among the low-, medium-, and high-fragmentation scenarios with equal habitat amount indicate that fragmentation per se can constrain regional migration independently of habitat amount. Its interaction with life history traits was consistent with demographic feedback involving seed-source reduction and delayed reproduction, which may progressively slow leading-edge dynamics and increase extinction risk. Maintaining connectivity and reproductive sources is essential to reduce demographic delays and support long-term persistence in fragmented forests.

items.title: Legacy effects of land use land cover change on species distribution dynamics: evidence from a landscape of diverse biogeographic crossroads
items.abstract: Context Land use and land cover (LULC) change is a key driver of biodiversity distribution, yet species responses vary among taxa, habitats, and regions. Because species responses are context-dependent, understanding how ecological characteristics and landscape history influence biodiversity distribution is essential for conservation planning. Objectives We evaluated how nearly two centuries of LULC change have influenced vertebrate distribution dynamics across Texas, USA, a landscape of biogeographic crossroads. We tested whether habitat specialization, taxonomic identity, conservation status, and ecoregional context better explain range expansion, contraction, and redistribution than landscape change metrics alone. Methods We compared historical and contemporary distributions of 100 native vertebrate species (mammals, birds, reptiles, and amphibians). Multi-temporal LULC datasets (1850–2023) were integrated with species occurrences, habitat associations, and ecoregional data to identify drivers of distribution range change. Results LULC change was spatially heterogeneous, driven by agricultural expansion, cropland abandonment, shrubland encroachment, and urbanization. Most species shifted ranges, with responses varying by habitat, taxon, and ecoregion. Habitat specialists, reptiles, and amphibians showed the greatest contractions, whereas birds were comparably stable or expanding, with responses differing among ecoregions. Habitat affinity, vertebrate class, and ecoregional identity were stronger predictors of range change than landscape transformation metrics alone. Conclusions LULC legacies set the environmental template and influence species distributions indirectly through ecological filtering, species-specific traits, and regional context rather than change magnitude alone. By linking historical landscape trajectories with contemporary biodiversity patterns, this study provides a useful template for understanding land use legacies, species redistribution, and community reassembly in diverse landscapes, emphasizing adaptive capacity and connectivity for conservation planning.

items.title: Habitat-shifting predatory and herbivorous reef fishes exhibit spatial partitioning despite shared biophysical drivers of seascape use
items.abstract: Context Climate change and anthropogenic stressors are degrading coastal biogenic habitats, disrupting the vital pathways fish use to shift from nearshore nurseries to offshore reef environments. Although fishes are critical for ecosystem health, spatial management rarely accounts for the interconnectedness of fish habitat needs across their life cycle. Objectives To examine and compare drivers of habitat use for subadult size classes of five habitat-shifting fishes from two feeding guilds: mesopredators and herbivores. To assess the multi-species suitability of existing management zones. Methods We used MaxEnt to model habitat suitability for our focal fishes across the Florida Keys, USA, and performed permutation analyses to compare habitat use patterns and drivers among species. We used predicted suitability maps to quantify suitability for 58 management zones. Results Benthic habitat type was the strongest driver, with patch- and aggregate-reefs emerging as the most suitable across species. Habitats were more moderately suitable for mesopredators across the nearshore-offshore gradient, while S. guacamaia stood out among the herbivores as preferring nearshore and mid-channel habitats over offshore habitats. We observed spatial partitioning, even among species with similar diets and preferred habitat types. All management zones were more suitable than the region-wide average, with restoration zones exhibiting higher predicted suitability than protection zones. Considering their high suitability for these species, patch reefs are underrepresented in current management practices. Conclusions Our findings highlight the need to preserve connected habitat corridors that span nearshore–offshore gradients, and we encourage practitioners to incorporate habitat suitability into site selection. To maximize ecosystem benefits, future work should consider the habitat and connectivity needs of a broader range of species and functional groups.

items.title: Cognitive and institutional barriers to effective natural resource management under global change
items.abstract: Many of the most challenging decisions facing natural resource managers today can be understood as time dependent. The concept of time-dependent decisions is useful when considering natural resource management decisions that are characterized by nonstationarity in the underlying ecological system, uncertainty surrounding key ecological relationships, efficacy of management interventions, and difficult trade-offs between the present and the future. In a time-dependent decision, the optimal action changes depending on when the decision is made. We surveyed literature from the fields of cognitive psychology, environmental decision-making, and natural resource management to identify a key set of cognitive and institutional barriers that prevent decision makers from recognizing their decisions as time dependent. This failure obscures the complexity of nonstationarity, uncertainty, and intertemporal choice in natural resource management and facilitates assumptions of stationarity and time independence. We used land acquisition in the context of climate change as an example to explore the barriers to effective time-dependent decision-making at both individual and institutional scales. Using a theoretical model of land acquisition, we quantified the value of accounting for time dependence by comparing the performance of time-dependent, nonstationary decision models with models that assume time independence and stationarity. We found that the conservation value of land acquisition decisions was significantly improved through the use of time-dependent optimization models and that this improvement increased as nonstationarity increased. Finally, explicitly recognizing the time dependence of many natural resource management decisions will help improve the utility of existing decision tools and frameworks.
